{{Short description|Topology of an ordered vector space}}
{{one source|date=June 2020}}

{{Distinguish|Order topology (topology)}}

In mathematics, specifically in [[order theory]] and [[functional analysis]], the '''order topology''' of an [[ordered vector space]] <math>(X, \leq)</math> is the finest [[locally convex]] [[topological vector space]] (TVS) [[topology]] on <math>X</math> for which every order interval is bounded, where an '''order interval''' in <math>X</math> is a set of the form <math>[a, b] := \left\{ z \in X : a \leq z \text{ and } z \leq b \right\}</math> where <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> belong to <math>X.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=204–214}} 

The order topology is an important topology that is used frequently in the theory of [[ordered topological vector space]]s because the topology stems directly from the algebraic and order theoretic properties of <math>(X, \leq),</math> rather than from some topology that <math>X</math> starts out having. 
This allows for establishing intimate connections between this topology and the algebraic and order theoretic properties of <math>(X, \leq).</math> 
For many [[ordered topological vector space]]s that occur in analysis, their topologies are identical to the order topology.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|p=204}} 

== Definitions ==

The family of all locally convex topologies on <math>X</math> for which every order interval is bounded is non-empty (since it contains the coarsest possible topology on <math>X</math>) and the order topology is the upper bound of this family.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=204–214}} 

A subset of <math>X</math> is a neighborhood of the origin in the order topology if and only if it is convex and absorbs every order interval in <math>X.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=204–214}} 
A neighborhood of the origin in the order topology is necessarily an [[absorbing set]] because <math>[x, x] := \{ x \}</math> for all <math>x \in X.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=204–214}} 

For every <math>a \geq 0,</math> let <math>X_a = \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} n [-a, a]</math> and endow <math>X_a</math> with its order topology (which makes it into a normable space). 
The set of all <math>X_a</math>'s is directed under inclusion and if <math>X_a \subseteq X_b</math> then the natural inclusion of <math>X_a</math> into <math>X_b</math> is continuous. 
If <math>X</math> is a [[regularly ordered]] vector space over the reals and if <math>H</math> is any subset of the positive cone <math>C</math> of <math>X</math> that is cofinal in <math>C</math> (e.g. <math>H</math> could be <math>C</math>), then <math>X</math> with its order topology is the inductive limit of <math>\left\{ X_a : a \geq 0 \right\}</math> (where the bonding maps are the natural inclusions).{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=230–234}}

The lattice structure can compensate in part for any lack of an order unit:

{{math theorem|name=Theorem{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=230–234}}|note=|style=|math_statement=
Let <math>X</math> be a [[vector lattice]] with a [[Regular order (mathematics)|regular order]] and let <math>C</math> denote its positive cone. Then the order topology on <math>X</math> is the finest locally convex topology on <math>X</math> for which <math>C</math> is a [[Normal cone (functional analysis)|normal cone]]; it is also the same as the [[Mackey topology]] induced on <math>X</math> with respect to the [[Dual system|duality]] <math>\left\langle X, X^{+} \right\rangle.</math>  
}}

In particular, if <math>(X, \tau)</math> is an ordered [[Fréchet lattice]] over the real numbers then <math>\tau</math> is the ordered topology on <math>X</math> if and only if the positive cone of <math>X</math> is a normal cone in <math>(X, \tau).</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=230–234}} 

If <math>X</math> is a regularly ordered [[vector lattice]] then the ordered topology is the finest locally convex TVS topology on <math>X</math> making <math>X</math> into a [[locally convex vector lattice]]. If in addition <math>X</math> is order complete then <math>X</math> with the order topology is a [[barreled space]] and every band decomposition of <math>X</math> is a topological direct sum for this topology.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=230–234}} 
In particular, if the order of a vector lattice <math>X</math> is regular then the order topology is generated by the family of all [[lattice seminorm]]s on <math>X.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=230–234}}

== Properties ==

Throughout, <math>(X, \leq)</math> will be an [[ordered vector space]] and <math>\tau_{\leq}</math> will denote the order topology on <math>X.</math> 

* The dual of <math>\left(X, \tau_{\leq}\right)</math> is the [[order bound dual]] <math>X_b</math> of <math>X.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=230–234}} 
* If <math>X_b</math> separates points in <math>X</math> (such as if <math>(X, \leq)</math> is regular) then <math>\left(X, \tau_{\leq}\right)</math> is a [[bornological]] locally convex TVS.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=230–234}} 
* Each [[positive linear operator]] between two ordered vector spaces is continuous for the respective order topologies.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=230–234}} 
* Each [[order unit]] of an ordered TVS is interior to the positive cone for the order topology.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=230–234}} 
* If the order of an ordered vector space <math>X</math> is a [[Regular order (mathematics)|regular order]] and if each positive sequence of [[Order summable|type <math>\ell^1</math>]] in <math>X</math> is [[order summable]], then <math>X</math> endowed with its order topology is a [[barreled space]].{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=230–234}} 
* If the order of an ordered vector space <math>X</math> is a [[Regular order (mathematics)|regular order]] and if for all <math>x \geq 0</math> and <math>y \geq 0</math> <math>[0, x] + [0, y] = [0, x + y]</math> holds, then the positive cone of <math>X</math> is a [[Normal cone (functional analysis)|normal cone]] in <math>X</math> when <math>X</math> is endowed with the order topology.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=230–234}}  In particular, the continuous dual space of <math>X</math> with the order topology will be the [[Order dual (functional analysis)|order dual]] <math>X</math><sup>+</sup>.
* If <math>(X, \leq)</math> is an [[Archimedean order]]ed vector space over the real numbers having an [[order unit]] and let <math>\tau_{\leq}</math> denote the order topology on <math>X.</math> Then <math>\left(X, \tau_{\leq}\right)</math> is an [[ordered TVS]] that is [[normable]], <math>\tau_{\leq}</math> is the finest locally convex TVS topology on <math>X</math> such that the positive cone is normal, and the following are equivalent:{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=230–234}} 
#<math>\left(X, \tau_{\leq}\right)</math> is complete.
#Each positive sequence of [[Order summable|type <math>\ell^1</math>]] in <math>X</math> is [[order summable]].
* In particular, if <math>(X, \leq)</math> is an [[Archimedean order]]ed vector space having an [[order unit]] then the order <math>\,\leq\,</math> is a regular order and <math>X_b = X^+.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=230–234}} 
* If <math>X</math> is a Banach space and an ordered vector space with an order unit then <math>X</math>'s topological is identical to the order topology if and only if the positive cone of <math>X</math> is a [[Normal cone (functional analysis)|normal cone]] in <math>X.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=230–234}}
* A [[vector lattice]] homomorphism from <math>X</math> into <math>Y</math> is a [[topological homomorphism]] when <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> are given their respective order topologies.{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=250-257}}

== Relation to subspaces, quotients, and products ==

If <math>M</math> is a [[Solid set|solid]] vector subspace of a [[vector lattice]] <math>X,</math> then the order topology of <math>X / M</math> is the quotient of the order topology on <math>X.</math>{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=250-257}}

== Examples ==

The order topology of a finite product of ordered vector spaces (this product having its canonical order) is identical to the product topology of the [[topological product]] of the constituent ordered vector spaces (when each is given its order topology).{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=230–234}}
